title: How HTML, CSS and JavaScript Work Together in a Modern Web Application
learningObjectives: Explain that HTML defines the meaning and structure of content, including headings, paragraphs, links, images, forms and buttons, rather than deciding the complete visual design or behaviour by itself.
Explain that CSS controls how HTML content is presented, including colours, fonts, text sizes, spacing, borders, alignment, responsive layout and visual states.
Explain that JavaScript adds behaviour and logic to a page, such as responding to clicks, validating form input, calculating values, showing messages and updating content.
Compare the distinct responsibilities of HTML, CSS and JavaScript and choose the appropriate technology for a content, appearance or interaction change.
Describe how a browser reads an HTML document, discovers linked CSS and JavaScript files, builds the page structure, applies styles and runs scripts to create the interactive page a user sees.
Identify the roles of index.html, styles.css and app.js in a small project and explain how an HTML link element and script element connect the files to the page.
Trace a simple button interaction from the HTML button, through a JavaScript event listener, to a change in the page content or state.
Explain how CSS selectors target HTML elements and how JavaScript can select and update page elements through the DOM without confusing those tasks with editing the original HTML file.
Organize a small project by keeping meaningful structure in HTML, presentation rules in CSS and interaction logic in JavaScript, while using clear file names and correct relative paths.
Make one small change at a time, save the relevant file, refresh or retest the page, and identify which technology is responsible if the expected result does not appear.
Recognize common integration mistakes such as a missing stylesheet link, incorrect script path, selector mismatch, JavaScript syntax error or event listener attached to the wrong element.
Explain why HTML, CSS and JavaScript work together as coordinated parts of one web page, while each has a different primary responsibility and none alone provides the full experience.

understand.concept: A web page usually combines three technologies with different primary responsibilities. HTML gives content its structure and meaning, CSS controls its presentation, and JavaScript adds behaviour and interaction. For example, HTML can provide a heading and button, CSS can arrange and style them, and JavaScript can respond when the button is selected. The browser coordinates these parts so they work as one page.
understand.whyItMatters: When you know which technology owns a task, you can make a change in the right place and investigate problems more efficiently. Keeping each technology focused on its main responsibility also makes a project easier to read, test and maintain. The roles are distinct, but they cooperate: CSS selects HTML elements, and JavaScript can access and update page elements through the Document Object Model (DOM).
understand.history: This lesson focuses on how the three technologies cooperate in a modern browser; detailed histories are covered in their dedicated lessons.
understand.analogy: Think of a theatre production. HTML establishes the scenes and the elements that exist, CSS controls their visual presentation, and JavaScript provides actions and responses that make the production interactive. The audience experiences one production even though different responsibilities contribute to it.
understand.analogyLimit: The comparison is only a memory aid. HTML, CSS and JavaScript can influence one another: JavaScript can change content or classes, CSS can respond to states, and HTML semantics affect accessibility and browser behaviour. Their technical roles are more flexible than separate theatre teams.

explain.narrative:
A browser begins with an HTML response and parses it into a document structure represented by the DOM. The document can reference stylesheets with link elements and scripts with script elements. CSS is parsed into rules that participate in the cascade and produce computed styles for matching elements. JavaScript executes according to its loading mode and can read or change the DOM, respond to events, request data and update application state. The browser coordinates these resources and rendering work; it does not simply display three separate files.

Keep the responsibilities clear. HTML should express meaningful structure and semantics: headings, navigation, forms, buttons, tables and landmarks. CSS should express presentation and responsive behaviour, including layout, typography, states and media queries. JavaScript should implement behaviour, state transitions, validation and communication with APIs. This separation is a maintainability guideline, not a claim that the technologies cannot interact. CSS selectors depend on document structure, JavaScript can change classes and content, and semantic HTML provides built-in browser behaviour and accessibility.

For an interaction, trace the full chain: the HTML supplies a real button; JavaScript selects it and registers an event listener; a user action dispatches an event; the handler updates the DOM or application state; and the browser recalculates the affected rendering output. A missing stylesheet, wrong script URL, selector mismatch, script timing problem, runtime exception or incorrect event handling can break a different link in this chain.

Use browser Developer Tools to identify the failing layer. Network confirms whether CSS and JavaScript resources loaded and which response they received. Elements shows the live DOM and matched styles. Console reveals script errors. Performance helps identify expensive work. Avoid using a clickable div when a native button provides the required keyboard and accessibility behaviour. Prefer semantic HTML first, then add CSS and JavaScript where they provide a real benefit.

examples.code:
Welcome

/* styles.css */ body { font-family: sans-serif; } button { padding: 8px 12px; } // app.js const button = document.querySelector("#messageButton"); button.addEventListener("click", () => { document.querySelector("#title").textContent = "Hello from JavaScript!"; });
examples.explanation: The HTML creates the heading and button and connects the other files. The CSS changes how the page looks. The JavaScript listens for a click and changes the heading text through the DOM. The browser combines these contributions into one interactive page. In a real project, put each part in its own file exactly as indicated.
examples.expectedOutput: The page shows a heading and a button. The button has CSS styling. When the user clicks it, the heading changes to “Hello from JavaScript!”.

examples.title: The browser-side responsibility map
examples.code:
HTML response → DOM
CSS files → CSS rules → cascade → computed styles
JavaScript → event handlers + application state + DOM updates
DOM + computed styles + assets → layout → paint → composite
examples.explanation: The three technologies have distinct primary roles, but their outputs cooperate. JavaScript can update structure or classes; CSS can respond to state; HTML semantics influence browser behaviour and accessibility.
examples.expectedOutput: You can identify which layer owns structure, presentation and behaviour, and where their integration points occur.

examples.title: Script loading affects when code can access the document
examples.code:
<!-- Preferred for many external page scripts -->
<script src="app.js" defer></script>

<!-- Runs when fetched; ordering is not guaranteed -->
<script src="analytics.js" async></script>

<!-- Module scripts are deferred by default -->
<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>
examples.explanation: defer downloads in parallel and runs after HTML parsing, preserving order among deferred classic scripts. async runs as soon as it is ready and does not guarantee order. Module scripts are deferred by default. Choose based on dependencies, not habit.
examples.expectedOutput: You can explain why a script may run before or after a DOM element is parsed.

examples.title: Use native HTML controls before adding behaviour
examples.code: const button = document.querySelector("#saveButton"); const status = document.querySelector("#status"); button.addEventListener("click", () => { status.textContent = "Saved"; });
examples.explanation: A native button supports keyboard activation and exposes button semantics. The status region can announce a dynamic update to assistive technology. A clickable generic element would require additional keyboard and accessibility work.
examples.expectedOutput: The button works with pointer and keyboard input and updates a status message.

examples.title: CSS selectors connect styles to document structure
examples.code:
<button class="primary" type="button">Continue</button>

.primary {
  background: #155e75;
  color: white;
}

.primary:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
examples.explanation: The class in HTML gives CSS a stable styling hook. The focus-visible state provides a visible keyboard focus indicator. Avoid styling through fragile selectors that depend on unrelated nesting.
examples.expectedOutput: The same semantic button receives the intended default and keyboard-focus presentation.

examples.title: Debug the connection between the three technologies
examples.code:
Network → Did the CSS and JS requests succeed?
Elements → Does the expected element exist?
Styles → Which rule wins in the cascade?
Console → Did JavaScript throw an exception?
Sources → Does the event handler run?
examples.explanation: A symptom can originate in another layer. For example, a correct CSS selector cannot style an element that is not present, and a correct event handler cannot run if the script failed to load.
examples.expectedOutput: You can use evidence to locate the broken integration point before editing code.

practise.guidedTask: Build a small accessible interaction with three separate files. In HTML, create a main landmark, a heading, a paragraph and a button with a descriptive accessible name. In CSS, create a responsive layout and visible keyboard focus style. In JavaScript, register an event listener that updates the paragraph and an aria-live status message. Test with mouse and keyboard. Then deliberately break the stylesheet path, script path and selector one at a time; use Network, Elements and Console to identify each failure.
practise.independentTask: Create a responsive task counter. HTML must provide semantic structure and a native button. CSS must handle layout, spacing, focus visibility and a reduced-motion preference. JavaScript must keep a numeric state, update the displayed count and prevent invalid values. Keep the files separate, document the interaction contract and test keyboard operation, narrow screens and repeated clicks.
hints: Check that the stylesheet path in the `link` element matches the actual file name and folder.
Check that the script path is correct; `defer` lets the browser run the script after the HTML has been parsed.
Use a CSS selector that matches the element's id or class exactly.
Use the browser Console to inspect JavaScript errors and test one change at a time.

questions.prompt: Which technology primarily defines the meaning and structure of headings, paragraphs and links?
questions.explanation: HTML describes page content and its structure and meaning.

questions.prompt: Which technology primarily controls colours, spacing, fonts and layout?
questions.explanation: CSS defines the presentation of HTML content.

questions.prompt: Which technology can respond to a button click and update page text?
questions.explanation: JavaScript can listen for events and update page content through the DOM.

questions.prompt: Why should a beginner keep HTML, CSS and JavaScript responsibilities organized?
options: It makes the project easier to understand, test and maintain
It prevents the browser from loading the page
It makes all three technologies identical
questions.answer: It makes the project easier to understand, test and maintain
questions.explanation: Clear separation of primary responsibilities improves readability and troubleshooting.

questions.prompt: Which script loading mode normally waits until HTML parsing has completed while preserving order among deferred classic scripts?
options: A script with no loading attribute always
questions.explanation: defer scripts are fetched in parallel and execute after parsing, in document order.

questions.prompt: Why is a native button usually preferable to a clickable div for an action?
options: A button automatically writes server code.
A button already provides native interactive semantics and keyboard behaviour.
questions.answer: A button already provides native interactive semantics and keyboard behaviour.
questions.explanation: Native controls provide built-in interaction semantics and reduce the extra work needed for accessibility.

questions.prompt: A click handler does not run and the script request returns 404. What should be fixed first?
options: The script URL or server path so the file loads.
questions.answer: The script URL or server path so the file loads.
questions.explanation: The browser cannot execute a script resource that it failed to retrieve.

questions.prompt: What is the cascade responsible for?
options: Selecting and resolving applicable CSS declarations into computed styles.
questions.answer: Selecting and resolving applicable CSS declarations into computed styles.
questions.explanation: The cascade determines which declarations apply when rules overlap, taking origin, importance, layers, specificity and source order into account.
